prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at the magic angle.

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a clear case of theory and experiment forming one story. The 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model predicted that the bands flatten at a small twist angle, and the 2018 Jarillo-Herrero experiments found correlated insulators and superconductivity in a pure carbon system, which nobody would have expected from simple band theory. This created a new tunable platform for correlated electrons, and the effect has been reproduced by many independent groups and in other moire materials. I have reconsidered my opening list in light of my colleagues' views. I now think a three-name credit including Bistritzer is the fairer attribution, because the flat-band prediction is a joint paper of Bistritzer and MacDonald. I would not name Cao or others as additional laureates because the prize can carry only three, and the proposal plus the decisive discovery are covered.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, the phase diagram is still moving, and Mehlig is right that eight years is short next to the older candidates. The credit is also contested: Cao and colleagues did the experimental work, Dean, Young, Yazdani, Efetov and others made key follow-ups, and earlier moire-band theory exists that I cannot verify. Against my own choice, optical lattice clocks have far more first-place support and are unquestionably mature, so I may be giving too much weight to my own field.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked KTHNY melting first as a clean, analytically controlled mechanism, and ranked magic-angle graphene fifth as possibly premature because the superconducting mechanism is unsettled.
responses.response: I take the prematurity point seriously and I do not dismiss it. I would answer that the discovery being cited is the existence of correlated insulators and superconductivity at the magic angle, not their microscopic origin, and that has been reproduced widely and quantitatively matched to the continuum theory. The same open-mechanism situation applied to high-Tc superconductors when they were rewarded. On KTHNY, I agree it is a beautiful theory, but I find the experimental confirmation less decisive and the overlap with the 2016 defect-and-topology prize a real obstacle. Only one member ranked it, so I do not see it as a leading candidate.

responses.point: Kroll ranked optical lattice clocks first as a clear, original measurement advance that is mature and reproduced in many labs, with the redefinition of the second pending.
responses.response: I agree with Kroll that the clocks are very mature and the science is robust, and this is why I rank them as my first alternative. My qualification is about novelty of the physical discovery rather than quality. The frequency comb (2005) and ion clocks (2012) already covered the metrology line, and the lattice clock is a refinement in precision. I ask whether it reveals new quantum behaviour or just better measurement. I would not oppose it if the committee wants a prize in precision measurement, but I do not accept that the strength of opening first places settles the matter.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED first as a foundational demonstration that supplies the architecture of superconducting processors, and noted a possible conflict through closeness to the field and to Chalmers.
responses.response: I appreciate Johansson's candour about the conflict. Scientifically, I ranked circuit QED last because of the strong thematic overlap with the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, which I chaired. Awarding the same area so soon would look like an unbalanced pattern, and the four-name credit forces an arbitrary omission of Blais or Girvin. Given your stated closeness to the credited people, I would suggest you do not lead the discussion on this entry.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked topological insulators first as a genuine discovery with a clear before and after, confirmed by many groups, and called recognition timely and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I agree on the quality and on the independent confirmation in 2D and 3D, and I ranked the entry sixth only because attribution looks unsolvable. Kane and Mele are clear, but Molenkamp as the third name leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang who proposed the HgTe realisation, and Hasan, Fu, Moore and Balents for the 3D case. I do not think we can give an attribution-clean answer here, and it also follows the 2016 topological prize closely. I keep it as an alternative and would reconsider if the committee finds a defensible three-person set.

responses.point: Olsson ranked magic-angle graphene fourth, saying the theory-then-experiment pairing is clean but recognition may be somewhat early and that the credit could be contested.
responses.response: I agree with Olsson that the Bistritzer-MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero pillars are the decisive ones, and Olsson, Johansson and Mehlig all name Bistritzer, which has moved me to include him. I disagree mildly that it is early: the correlated phases have had seven years of independent confirmation, and the field has already produced fractional Chern insulators and related states in moire systems, so its lasting impact is visible.

uncertainties: Whether the superconducting pairing mechanism being unresolved should delay recognition of the magic-angle discovery.
Whether the committee prefers the three-name credit with Bistritzer, or the two-name theory-plus-experiment pair I proposed at opening.
Whether a clear majority for optical lattice clocks should outweigh my judgement on novelty, and whether that candidate has a clean enough separation from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
I cannot independently verify priority for earlier moire-band theory or for parallel experimental groups.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile with any of the credited candidates on the shortlist (MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, or the alternatives). My ties are to Uppsala, Los Alamos co-authors and committee colleagues, none of whom are credited on these ballots. I note that I chaired the committee for the 2025 prize.
